title: Why the Color on Your Screen Is Never Exactly the Color on the Jersey
meta_title: Screen vs Fabric: Why Jersey Colors Shift | MOMUTO
meta_descript: A screen color cannot be matched 1:1 on fabric: printers use Pantone references and ink soaks into white polyester. What shifts, and what MOMUTO does about it.
author: MOMUTO
content:
Kit Buying Guide
Key Answer

A color on a screen cannot be reproduced one-to-one on fabric. Screens emit light in RGB; a sublimation printer works from Pantone-style ink references, not hex codes, and the ink is absorbed by a white polyester fabric, so every color translates into something slightly different. A small shift is normal on every custom jersey from every maker. What changes between makers is what they do about it. At MOMUTO: designs are steered towards colors that translate well, a designer flags an unrealistic concept before it is recreated, and every order goes through our own print test in 3–4 shades before production.

Of all the complaints custom-kit buyers leave online, one comes up for every brand: "the color was different from what I saw on screen". It is usually true, and it is usually nobody's fault. Here is what happens between a screen and a jersey, and what a maker can do to keep the two as close as possible.

Three reasons the color moves

  1. A screen emits light; a jersey reflects it. Your monitor builds color from red, green and blue light (a hex code like #1E3A8A). Fabric has no light of its own: it reflects the room. A luminous screen blue and the same blue on a jersey under a floodlight are two different physical things.
  2. Printers do not speak hex. A dye-sublimation printer works from ink references (Pantone-style swatches and the printer's own profiles). Every hex code has to be mapped to the nearest printable reference, and some screen colors, especially neon greens, electric blues and very saturated reds, have no exact equivalent in ink.
  3. The ink is absorbed, not laid on top. Sublimation turns the ink into gas that bonds with white polyester fibers. The color you get is the ink inside a white fabric, which is why it never peels, and also why it is always a shade off the pure screen value.

Every custom-kit maker, from the biggest to the smallest, works inside these three limits. Which is why the honest answer to "will it match my screen?" is: closely, not perfectly.

What MOMUTO does about it

We cannot change physics, so we take the measures that reduce the gap. Three of them:

  • Colors we know will translate. Our Ready to Play designs and the colorways in the 3D designer use colors we have printed many times. Unrealistic brightness and contrast are avoided at the source.
  • A designer tells you before we recreate your concept. Many concepts now arrive as AI renders, and AI loves colors that only exist on a screen: glowing, neon, impossibly saturated. When a mockup is not realistic in this sense, our designer says so and proposes the closest version that prints well, before anything is produced.
  • Our own print test on every order. Before production, your design is printed in three or four shades and we keep the one that reflects the design best. It is not a 1:1 guarantee; it is the step that removes most of the surprises.
"A screen can't be matched one to one on fabric. It's simply not possible: the printer works with Pantone references, not hex codes, and the ink is absorbed by a white fabric, so every color translates into something. What we can do is reduce the disappointment: we steer designs towards colors we know translate well, our designers flag a concept that isn't realistic before we recreate it, and every order goes through our own print test, three or four shades, and we keep the one that reflects the design best."
— Alberto, founder of MOMUTO

What you can do as a team

  • Give us a reference, not a feeling. If a color is critical (a club blue, a sponsor red), send the Pantone code or a physical item in that color. We match the print to the reference, not to your screen.
  • Avoid neon and glowing tones if an exact match matters to you. Deep blues, reds, greens, black and white translate the most faithfully.
  • Look at the mockup on two screens (phone and laptop) before approving it. If they already disagree with each other, the fabric will sit somewhere in between.
  • Know what is covered. A slight tone difference is normal and not a defect; a kit that differs from the approved mockup is, and is replaced (see our returns policy).

The rest of what makes a jersey good or bad, the fabric itself, is covered in what are soccer jerseys made of and on our printing and materials page.

Frequently asked questions

Will my jersey match the color on my screen?
Closely, not perfectly. Screens emit light and fabric reflects it, printers use Pantone-style references rather than hex codes, and the ink is absorbed by white polyester. A slight shift is normal on every custom jersey. MOMUTO prints each order in 3–4 shades before production and keeps the closest.
Which colors print most faithfully on a jersey?
Deep blues, reds, greens, black and white. Neon greens, electric blues and very saturated reds have no exact ink equivalent and shift the most.
Can I give a Pantone code for my team color?
Yes. Send the Pantone reference or a physical item in that color and the print is matched to the reference, not to your screen.
Is a color difference a defect I can return?
A slight tone difference between screen and fabric is normal and not a defect. A kit that differs from the approved mockup is, and is replaced.
What does MOMUTO do to keep colors close?
Designs use colors known to translate well, a designer flags an unrealistic concept before recreating it, and every order goes through an in-house print test in 3–4 shades before production.
